title: Heaps and Priority Queues
relevance: Heaps and priority queues underpin classic SDE/OA patterns: Top-K selection, merge-k streams, streaming medians, and greedy scheduling.

phases.goal: Establish what a heap is, the heap-order property, and why it maps to a flat array.

must_hit.point: A heap is a complete binary tree that satisfies the heap-order property.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States both completeness and heap-order, not just 'a binary tree of priorities'.

must_hit.point: In a max-heap every parent is >= its children; in a min-heap every parent is <= its children.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Correctly distinguishes max-heap vs min-heap ordering.

must_hit.point: A complete binary tree is filled on all levels except possibly the lowest, which is filled from the left, so a heap can be stored as a flat array without pointers.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions left-filled lowest level and array representation without child pointers.

must_hit.point: For 0-indexed array index i: left child at 2i+1, right child at 2i+2, parent at floor((i-1)/2).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Recites the three index formulas for 0-based layout.

probes: What is a heap, and why can we store it in an array without pointers?

hints.1: Think about the shape constraint plus the parent-vs-children value rule.
hints.2: Complete binary trees have no gaps, so children land at fixed offsets from index i.
hints.3: Definition: complete binary tree + heap-order; 0-based: left 2i+1, right 2i+2, parent floor((i-1)/2).

phases.goal: Explain insert, extract-root, build-heap, heap sort, and std::priority_queue defaults.

must_hit.point: Insert appends at the end then restores order by bubble-up/sift-up in O(log n) because tree height is logarithmic.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes append-then-swap-with-parent until order holds, cites O(log n).

must_hit.point: Extract-root replaces the root with the last element, shrinks size by 1, then restores order by sift-down/heapify in O(log n).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes last-to-root replacement and swapping with largest (max-heap) or smallest (min-heap) child.

must_hit.point: Bottom-up build-heap starts at the last internal node and heapifies backward to the root, running in O(n), not O(n log n).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names bottom-up heapify-from-last-internal-node and insists on O(n).

must_hit.point: Heap sort builds a max-heap, then repeatedly swaps the root with the last heap element, shrinks the heap, and heapifies the new root for n-1 rounds; it is O(n log n) time, O(1) auxiliary space, and not stable.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Covers build, swap-to-end loop, complexities, and non-stability.

must_hit.point: C++ std::priority_queue<int> is a max-heap by default; a min-heap needs an explicit container and std::greater<int>.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Flags the default max-heap surprise and the greater comparator pattern.

probes: Walk through insert and extract-min on an array heap. Why is bottom-up build-heap O(n)?

hints.1: Start from how the array stays complete, then how order is repaired after insert vs delete.
hints.2: Contrast one-by-one inserts with heapifying internal nodes from the bottom; most nodes sit near the leaves.
hints.3: Append+bubble-up and last-to-root+sift-down are O(log n); bottom-up build is O(n) because half the nodes are leaves (height 0) with almost no sift work.

phases.goal: Compare construction strategies, Top-K heap vs alternatives, and which heap polarity fits which query.

must_hit.point: Building by inserting one by one is O(n log n); the optimal bottom-up approach is O(n) because most nodes are near the bottom with small sift-down distance.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts the two build costs and explains the geometric bottom-heavy work argument.

must_hit.point: For the k-th largest, a size-k min-heap guarantees O(n log k); QuickSelect averages O(n) but can hit O(n^2) worst case.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States heap guarantee vs QuickSelect average/worst-case split.

must_hit.point: k-th largest uses a min-heap of size k; k-th smallest uses a max-heap of size k.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Correctly pairs polarity of heap with largest vs smallest query.

must_hit.point: Heap sort is in-place with O(1) auxiliary space and O(n log n) time, but it is not a stable sort.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions in-place/O(1) aux and explicitly that stability is lost.

probes: When would you use a size-k min-heap versus QuickSelect for the k-th largest? Why is build-heap linear?

hints.1: Compare guaranteed bounds versus average-case faster algorithms.
hints.2: Think about which end of the ordered set the heap root represents when the heap is capped at size k.
hints.3: Size-k min-heap traps the largest k and the root is the k-th largest in O(n log k); QuickSelect is O(n) average / O(n^2) worst; bottom-up build is O(n).

phases.goal: Map interview patterns to the right heap setup: Top-K, merge-k, two-heaps median, and greedy merges.

must_hit.point: K-th / Top-K: keep a bounded heap of size k so the root is the k-th extreme among the elite k.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes streaming into a size-k heap and reading the root as the answer.

must_hit.point: Merging k sorted streams uses a min-heap of size k holding the current front of each stream; overall time O(N log k) for N total elements.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says heap of heads, pop min then push next from that list, cites O(N log k).

must_hit.point: Running median: max-heap for the lower half and min-heap for the upper half, keeping a size difference of at most 1.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names two heaps with roles and the balance invariant.

must_hit.point: Minimum cost to connect sticks: repeatedly extract the two shortest via a min-heap, pay their sum, and push the fused stick back (Huffman-style).
must_hit.evidence_hint: States greedy two-shortest merges managed by a min-heap.

probes: How do you find a running median from a stream? How do you merge k sorted lists efficiently?

hints.1: Ask which end of each half you need in O(1) after each insertion.
hints.2: For streams of lists, you only need the current heads under comparison at once.
hints.3: Two heaps: max-heap lower half + min-heap upper half, size gap at most 1; merge-k: min-heap of size k of list heads, O(N log k).

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Inserting n elements one by one is O(n log n). Bottom-up heapify from the last internal node to the root is O(n), because half the nodes are leaves (height 0), a quarter sit at height 1, and so on, so total sift work converges linearly.

tradeoffs.topic: Size-k heap vs QuickSelect for k-th largest
tradeoffs.strong_answer: A min-heap of size k yields a strict O(n log k) bound. QuickSelect averages O(n) but can degrade to O(n^2); the heap answer is preferred when a reliable bound matters.

tradeoffs.topic: Min-heap of size k vs max-heap of size k
tradeoffs.strong_answer: k-th largest / top-k largest keep a min-heap of size k (root is the smallest of the large set). k-th smallest keeps a max-heap of size k (root is the largest of the small set).

tradeoffs.topic: Heap sort stability and space vs other O(n log n) sorts
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Heap sort is O(n log n) time with O(1) auxiliary space (in-place) but is not stable, so it loses when relative order of equal keys must be preserved.

tradeoffs.topic: Merge-all-then-sort vs min-heap of k heads
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Dumping every node and sorting costs O(N log N). A min-heap of the k current heads merges in O(N log k) while using O(k) heap space.

gotchas.correction: It is a max-heap by default; a min-heap needs std::priority_queue<int, std::vector<int>, std::greater<int>>.

gotchas.trap: Writing a custom comparator with 'normal' less-than intuition.
gotchas.correction: operator() should return true when the first argument has lower priority than the second; returning true pushes that element further down the extraction order.

gotchas.trap: Using a max-heap for the k-th largest (or a min-heap for the k-th smallest).
gotchas.correction: k-th largest needs a min-heap of size k; k-th smallest needs a max-heap of size k.

gotchas.trap: Claiming bottom-up build-heap is O(n log n) like n inserts.
gotchas.correction: Bottom-up build-heap is O(n); most nodes are near the bottom with small maximum sift-down distance.

gotchas.trap: Thinking 'convert min-heap to max-heap' must exploit the existing min-heap structure specially.
gotchas.correction: The min-heap label is misdirection—treat it as an array and run bottom-up max-heapify in O(n).

gotchas.trap: Forgetting heap sort is unstable despite being in-place.
gotchas.correction: Heap sort is O(n log n) with O(1) auxiliary space but is not a stable sort.
